And parallel lines receding from the viewer appear to converge at a **vanishing point** on it. **The systems** are named for how many vanishing points the main planes use: - **One-point**: the object's front face is parallel to the picture plane, and only the receding edges converge, to a single point. The road, corridor and railway view. - **Two-point**: you see a corner, so two sets of horizontal edges converge to two points on the horizon. Verticals stay vertical. The standard view of a building. - **Three-point**: add a vanishing point far above or below for the verticals, which is what happens when you look sharply up or down. The tall building from street level. **Practical rules that do most of the work:** - Everything above the horizon is above your eye; you see its underside. Everything below it, you see the top of. On a row of identical people, every head sits on the horizon regardless of distance. - ⚠️ **Do not space repeating elements by guesswork** — fence posts, windows, floor tiles. The correct method is the diagonal: draw a diagonal through the rectangle you have, and where it crosses the midline gives you the next division. Evenly spaced guesses look wrong immediately. - **Foreshortening** is the compression of a form pointing toward the viewer, and it is the hardest thing to draw because the symbol library objects loudly. Measure it; trust the measurement over the feeling that an arm cannot possibly be that short. **Atmospheric or aerial perspective** is the other half and is often more persuasive than the geometry. With distance, contrast falls, edges soften, detail drops, and colours shift toward the colour of the air — usually cooler and bluer. Reducing contrast in the background does more for depth than any amount of correct convergence. **Overlap** is the simplest depth cue of all and the strongest: an object in front of another is unambiguously nearer. **When to break it.** Perspective describes a single fixed viewpoint with one eye. Plenty of great art ignores it deliberately — much of it predates the system entirely. Learn it so that departing from it is a choice.

sections.heading: Colour: What Actually Governs It
sections.body: Colour is the area with the most folklore attached, so it is worth separating what is physically true from what is a teaching convention. **Three properties describe any colour.** **Hue** is its position around the wheel — red, green, blue. **Saturation** or chroma is its intensity, from vivid to grey. **Value** is its lightness. ⚠️ Beginners think about hue and ignore value, which is the wrong way round: **value does the structural work**, and a painting with correct values and approximate hues reads far better than the reverse. **Two colour systems, and confusing them causes most of the trouble.** **Additive** mixing applies to light — screens, stage lighting — with primaries red, green and blue, combining to white. **Subtractive** mixing applies to pigment, where each layer absorbs part of the spectrum; printing uses cyan, magenta and yellow. ⚠️ The traditional artist's primaries of **red, yellow and blue** are a teaching convention, not a physical fact — they cannot mix the full gamut, and a cyan-magenta- yellow set mixes a substantially wider range. Nothing about that makes the traditional wheel useless; just do not treat it as physics. **Complementary colours** sit opposite one another and are the most useful practical tool on the wheel. Placed side by side they intensify each other; **mixed together they neutralise**, which is how you grey a colour without reaching for black. Mixing with black usually deadens and often shifts the hue unpleasantly — mixing with the complement produces a far livelier grey. **Temperature.** Reds, oranges and yellows read as warm and advance; blues and blue-greens read as cool and recede. Temperature is relative — a warm blue exists — and the warm–cool relationship between light and shadow is one of the strongest tools in painting. A common observation: warm light produces cool shadows, and cool light produces warm ones. **Workable schemes.** Monochromatic; analogous, using neighbours on the wheel; complementary; split-complementary, which is easier to control; triadic. A widely used proportion is roughly **60/30/10** — a dominant, a supporting and an accent — and its value is mostly that it stops the beginner error of giving everything equal weight. **Limited palettes teach faster than full ones.** Three colours plus white forces you to mix, which is how you actually learn colour relationships, and it guarantees harmony because everything shares its parents. ⚠️ **A caution about colour psychology.** The claim that particular colours reliably cause particular emotions is far weaker than popular writing suggests. Associations are heavily cultural — white means mourning in some societies and celebration in others — and context dominates. Use it as convention, not law.

sections.heading: Composition: Arranging What the Viewer Sees
sections.body: Composition is the arrangement of elements within the frame, and it is where a technically accurate picture becomes a good one or fails to. **Start with the format.** Landscape, portrait or square is a decision, not a default, and it sets the mood before anything is drawn. **The classic devices**, best understood as tendencies rather than rules: - **The rule of thirds**: dividing the frame in thirds and placing points of interest near the intersections. It is a simplification of older ideas about dynamic division, it works, and it is not a law. - **The golden ratio** and related proportional schemes. ⚠️ Its historical prevalence in art is routinely overstated, and claims that particular masterpieces were built on it are often applied after the fact. - **Leading lines** guide the eye into and through the picture — a road, a river, a fence, a gaze. - **Framing** an element with something in the foreground. - **The focal point**: one place the picture is about, established by contrast — of value, of colour saturation, of detail, of edge sharpness, or by being the point everything else points at. ⚠️ Making everything interesting makes nothing interesting. - **Balance**, symmetrical for stability and formality, asymmetrical for energy. - **Negative space** as an active element rather than leftover. **The value pattern is the composition.** Before rendering anything, a small rough sketch — a **thumbnail**, a few centimetres across, resolving the whole picture into three or four values — tells you whether it works. If the thumbnail is dull, the finished piece will be dull with more effort attached. Doing several thumbnails in different arrangements is the single highest-return habit available, and almost nobody does it. **Directing the eye.** Composition is control over where the viewer looks first, second and third, and how long they stay. Strong contrast, faces, sharp edges and convergence all attract attention; one should win. ⚠️ **Avoid**: the horizon cutting the frame exactly in half by accident; a subject centred without reason; tangents, where two edges just touch and create an unintended shape or flatten depth; and lines that lead the eye out of the frame with nothing to bring it back. **Cropping is composition.** Photographers know this and draughtsmen forget it. Cutting a picture after the fact is a legitimate compositional act, and a **viewfinder** — two L-shaped cards, or your hands — used before you start saves discovering it afterwards. **Test it.** Turn the picture upside down, or look at it in a mirror, or squint until it becomes a value pattern. All three break your familiarity and show you the arrangement rather than the subject.

sections.heading: Painting: Media and How They Behave
sections.body: Choosing a medium is largely choosing how much time you want before the paint stops moving, and how it will look when it stops. **Watercolour** is transparent, worked light to dark, with the white of the paper doing the work that white paint does elsewhere. It is unforgiving because you cannot easily take paint away — the discipline is in planning where the paper stays untouched. **Wet-on-wet** gives soft merged edges; **wet-on-dry** gives crisp ones; **glazing** is a transparent layer over a dry one; **lifting** removes pigment with a damp brush. Paper weight matters more than anything else: thin paper buckles, and heavy paper or stretched paper does not. **Acrylic** dries fast, is water-based, and once dry is waterproof and can be painted over indefinitely. That makes it the most forgiving and the most beginner-friendly, and its speed is also its main annoyance — blending on the canvas requires working quickly, a wet palette, or retarder. It can be thinned to behave somewhat like watercolour or used thickly like oil. **Oil** dries slowly by oxidation over days, which is precisely why it is the traditional choice for careful blending and subtle transitions. Its rules matter for permanence: **fat over lean** — each layer more oil-rich than the one beneath — and thick over thin, or the surface cracks as it cures. ⚠️ Solvents need ventilation; oily rags can spontaneously combust and must be spread flat to dry or stored in water. **Gouache** is opaque watercolour, matte, reworkable, and popular in illustration and design. **Pastel** is nearly pure pigment, brilliant and fragile, needing fixative and glazing. **Ink** ranges from line to wash. **Digital** removes material constraints — infinite undo, layers, free colour adjustment — and imposes its own: an unlimited canvas, and no natural stopping point. **Principles that cross all of them.** - **Work fat over lean, thick over thin, light over dark or dark over light — but pick one.** - **Big brushes for longer than feels comfortable.** Beginners reach for small brushes and detail far too early, which produces a fussy picture with no structure. - **Block in the large value masses first**, then adjust, then detail. Detail is the last five per cent and cannot substitute for the first ninety-five. - **Step back regularly.** Nearly every problem is visible from three metres and invisible at arm's length. - **Know when to stop.** Overworking is a far more common way to ruin a picture than stopping too early.

sections.heading: Drawing People: Proportion, Gesture and Faces
sections.body: The human figure is the hardest common subject, for a specific and diagnosable reason: everyone is an expert on what people look like, so errors that would pass unnoticed on a tree are glaring on a face. **Proportion, as a starting scaffold.** Adult figures are conventionally measured in head-heights, commonly given as about **seven and a half** for a realistic figure, with eight used for a more idealised one and longer still in fashion illustration. Useful landmarks: the midpoint of the standing body is roughly at the pubic bone, not the waist; elbows sit near the waist; fingertips reach mid-thigh; the knee is about halfway down the leg. ⚠️ Children are not small adults — the head is far larger relative to the body, roughly four head-heights in a toddler, and getting that ratio wrong is why amateur drawings of children look like shrunken adults. **The face.** The eyes sit at roughly the **vertical midpoint of the head**, which is the single most commonly violated proportion — beginners place them far too high, because the symbol library underestimates the cranium. Other conventions: about one eye's width between the eyes; the bottom of the nose roughly halfway from brow to chin; the mouth about a third of the way from nose to chin; the ears spanning roughly brow to nose base. Treat all of these as a starting armature to be corrected against the actual person. **Gesture before structure.** Find the line of action — the single sweeping curve of the pose — and the balance, before any anatomy. A figure drawn accurately in every part but with no gesture looks stiff and dead; a loose drawing with the right gesture reads as alive. **Contrapposto**, weight on one leg with the hips and shoulders tilting in opposition, is the most common standing pose in art because it is what people actually do. **Construction.** Simplify the body into masses — the ribcage and pelvis as two boxes connected by a flexible spine, limbs as cylinders — and pose those before adding surface. It handles foreshortening and rotation far better than drawing the outline. **Anatomy** is worth learning at the level of the major masses and landmarks — the bones you can see and feel — rather than every muscle. Landmarks are reliable because they do not change with pose or weight: the clavicle, the sternum's pit, the iliac crest, the knee's structures, the wrist, the ankle bones and their offset heights. **Hands and feet** are notoriously hard and the fix is unglamorous: draw a lot of them, from life, simplified into the palm mass plus fingers rather than five separate tubes. **Life drawing** teaches faster than anything else, because a real body under real light is the one reference that never hands you a symbol.

sections.heading: Graphic Design: Type, Hierarchy and Layout
sections.body: Design differs from art in having a job. A poster that is beautiful and does not communicate has failed, and the criteria are correspondingly more testable. **Hierarchy is the first principle.** The viewer should know instantly what to read first, second and third. Hierarchy is built by size, weight, colour, contrast, position and space. ⚠️ If everything is emphasised, nothing is, and this is the single commonest failure in amateur design. **The four principles that cover most of it**, from the design literature's standard summary: - **Proximity**: related things go near each other; unrelated things get space. Grouping does the work that lines and boxes are usually asked to do. - **Alignment**: nothing is placed arbitrarily. Every element aligns with something else, and a strong left edge beats scattered centring almost every time. - **Repetition**: repeat visual elements — a colour, a rule, a typeface, a spacing unit — to bind a piece together and make it feel designed. - **Contrast**: if two things are different, make them clearly different. Slightly different reads as a mistake. **Type.** A **serif** has finishing strokes; a **sans serif** does not; the claim that one is inherently more readable in print has weak evidence, and legibility depends far more on size, spacing and quality of setting. Practical rules that reliably help: limit yourself to **one or two typefaces**, and pair by contrast rather than similarity; keep body text at a comfortable size with **line spacing of roughly 1.4 to 1.6** times the type size; keep **line length** to something like 45–75 characters, because long lines make the eye lose its place returning; ⚠️ avoid setting long passages in all capitals, in italics, or in a light weight on a dark background, all of which slow reading measurably. **Kerning** is the space between specific letter pairs; **tracking** is uniform letter spacing; **leading** is the space between lines. **White space is not wasted space.** It is the main tool for creating hierarchy and calm, and the instinct to fill every corner is what makes amateur layouts feel frantic. **Grids** — columns and consistent margins — are why professional layouts feel coherent. Establish one, align to it, and depart from it deliberately for emphasis. **Colour in design** carries function: brand, state, and above all **contrast for legibility**. ⚠️ Accessibility is a real constraint rather than a nicety — a substantial share of people have some colour vision deficiency, so information must never be conveyed by colour alone, and text needs genuine luminance contrast against its background, not merely a different hue. **Logos** work when they are simple, memorable, appropriate, and legible at a centimetre across and in one colour. Test every logo in black and white and at thumbnail size; most amateur logos fail both.

sections.heading: Photography as Picture-Making
sections.body: A camera automates the recording and leaves the picture-making entirely to you, so most of what makes a photograph good is the composition and light already described. **The exposure triangle** is the technical core. **Aperture** — the f-number — controls how much light enters and, crucially, the **depth of field**: a wide aperture with a low number gives a shallow zone of sharpness and a blurred background, a narrow one keeps everything sharp. **Shutter speed** controls duration: fast freezes motion, slow blurs it deliberately and shows camera shake accidentally. **ISO** is sensitivity: higher lets you shoot in less light at the cost of noise. Change one and you must compensate with another, which is the whole of manual exposure. **Focal length** changes more than magnification. A wide lens exaggerates depth and makes near things loom; a long lens compresses distance and flattens. ⚠️ The apparent distortion in close-range portraits is a function of **how close you are**, not the lens itself — the fix is to step back and use a longer focal length. **Light is the subject.** The direction, quality and colour of light do more for a photograph than any equipment. **Soft** light from a large or diffused source flatters and reveals form gently; **hard** light from a small source gives sharp shadows and drama. **Side light** reveals texture and form; **front light** flattens; **back light** gives rims and silhouettes. The **golden hour** after sunrise and before sunset is warm and low, and **blue hour** is the cool twilight that follows. Overcast is a giant softbox and is excellent for portraits. **Metering and its failures.** ⚠️ A camera meters toward a mid grey, so it underexposes snow and overexposes a dark scene. **Exposure compensation** is the correction, and the **histogram** is a more reliable check than the screen. Highlights that are completely blown carry no recoverable information; shadows usually do. **Composition in a viewfinder.** The same devices apply — thirds, leading lines, framing, negative space — plus two of the camera's own: watching the background as carefully as the subject, since poles and branches grow out of heads only in photographs; and moving your feet, which is the most neglected technique in the medium. **Editing** is part of the process and always has been. Raw files hold more latitude than compressed ones. Sensible order: correct exposure and white balance, crop and straighten, adjust contrast and colour, then local adjustments, then sharpen last. ⚠️ **Ethics.** Editing for tone is normal; adding or removing content changes what the photograph claims. In journalism and documentary that line is a professional rule, and for photographs of people, permission — legal in some places, courteous everywhere — matters.

sections.heading: Practice, Reference and Getting Better
sections.body: Improvement in visual art is unusually well understood and unusually badly executed, because the methods that feel productive are not the ones that work. **Volume first, in the beginning.** Early on, quantity beats deliberation: the sheer number of drawings is what builds the perceptual and motor foundation. The commonly repeated advice to fill sketchbooks is right for the first stage. **Then deliberate practice.** Past the beginning, undirected drawing plateaus, because you practise what you can already do. Progress comes from identifying a specific weakness — hands, values, backgrounds, perspective — and working at the edge of your ability on that one thing, with feedback. This is less enjoyable than drawing what you like, which is precisely why most people plateau. **Use reference, without shame and without tracing.** ⚠️ Working from imagination alone tends to reinforce your symbols, which is the original problem. Drawing from life is the strongest reference because it gives depth, edges and light that photographs flatten. Photographs are the practical substitute; be aware they lie about tonal range, edges and lens distortion. **Copying master drawings** is a centuries-old training method and remains excellent, provided the results are labelled as studies. **Studies versus finished work.** Most practice should be studies — a hand, a fold, a colour relationship, a value pattern — not finished pieces. A finished piece takes far longer and teaches less per hour. **Getting useful feedback.** Ask a specific question — "does this read as three-dimensional?", "is the focal point where I think it is?" — because "what do you think?" gets politeness. Look at your own work in a mirror, upside down, at thumbnail size, and after a week away; all four defeat familiarity. Compare against your own work from a year ago, not against the best artists alive. **Habits that compound.** A small sketchbook carried everywhere. Timed exercises with a hard stop. A single subject drawn repeatedly over months. Studying pictures you like closely enough to work out *why* they work, which is a distinct skill from making them. ⚠️ **On plateaus and comparison.** Progress is stepwise, not smooth, and periods where nothing seems to improve usually precede a jump. The specific hazard of modern practice is comparing your work against an endless feed of the best work in the world, produced by people with far more hours — it is a reliable way to quit for no good reason. **On generative tools**, briefly and honestly: they will produce images, and they will not build perception. If the goal is to be able to see and make, the hours remain the hours.

sections.heading: How to Look at Pictures
sections.body: Looking at art is a skill, distinct from making it, and worth having on its own — most people spend seconds in front of a picture and conclude they do not respond to art, when what happened is that they did not look. **Slow down first.** The measured average time a gallery visitor spends with a work is famously short, well under half a minute. Almost everything worth having from a picture arrives after that. Pick a few works and give them ten minutes each rather than walking a whole museum. **A sequence that works:** 1. **Describe** before judging. What is literally there — objects, people, colours, marks? Saying it out loud is oddly effective at slowing the reflex to evaluate. 2. **Analyse** the arrangement. Where does your eye go first, and what took it there? What is the value pattern? What is emphasised, and how? 3. **Interpret**. What might it be about? What does the treatment — not the subject — suggest? 4. **Judge**, last, and separately from whether you like it. "Does this achieve what it appears to attempt?" is a different question from "does this appeal to me?", and keeping them apart is most of what art criticism is. **Notice the making.** Step close: brushwork, layering, pentimenti where the artist changed their mind, the weave of the canvas, the marks of the tool. Then step back. Alternating is how painters look at paintings. **Context helps, once you have looked.** When and where it was made, what it was for, who paid for it, what it would have cost, what conventions it obeyed or broke. An altarpiece, a court portrait and a modern gallery piece were made for wholly different purposes, and judging one by another's standards produces nonsense. **Scale and surface do not survive reproduction.** A photograph of a picture loses size, texture, sheen and the physical presence of the paint — which is why seeing the original matters and why work that reads as underwhelming in a book can be overwhelming in a room. ⚠️ **On "my child could do that."** It is worth taking seriously rather than dismissing, and the useful answer is that it is usually an argument about what art is *for*. Much twentieth-century work deliberately abandoned technical difficulty as the measure, asking questions about representation, materials and the institution instead. You are entitled to think that a mistake — but the disagreement is about the goal, not about competence, and finding out what the work was attempting is a precondition for the argument. **Trust your response, and interrogate it.** Both. Liking something is data; understanding why turns it into taste.

sections.heading: A Short History of Seeing, and Why Styles Change
sections.body: Styles are usually taught as a sequence of names. They make far more sense as a series of answers to changing questions about what a picture is for. **Before the Renaissance**, much European painting was not attempting optical realism at all. Byzantine and medieval images used scale for importance rather than distance, gold grounds instead of skies, and rigid conventions — because the picture's job was devotional and instructive, and depicting a sacred subject in a fixed, recognisable form was the point. **The Renaissance** made the picture a window. Linear perspective, anatomy from dissection, observed light, and the individual patron and portrait all belong to the same shift toward describing the visible world accurately. **Baroque** intensified it with drama, movement and extreme light and shade. **The nineteenth century** brought the change that reorganised everything: **photography**. Once a machine could record appearance cheaply and perfectly, the argument that painting's job was accurate description collapsed. What followed was not a decline in skill but a search for what else painting could do. **Impressionism** pursued light and the momentary sensation, with visible marks and colour used optically. **Post-Impressionism** went further into structure and emotion. **The twentieth century** pursued that logic to its limits. **Cubism** dismantled the single viewpoint that perspective had established. **Expressionism** subordinated appearance to feeling. **Abstraction** dispensed with the subject. **Dada and conceptual art** questioned whether the object mattered at all compared with the idea. Each is intelligible as an answer to "what is left for a picture to do that a camera cannot?" **Non-Western traditions** answered different questions entirely and should not be filed as stages in this story. Chinese landscape painting used shifting viewpoints, empty space as an active element, and calligraphic brushwork valued in itself. Islamic art developed geometry, pattern and calligraphy to extraordinary depth. Japanese printmaking's flat colour, bold cropping and outline influenced European painting profoundly in the nineteenth century — the traffic ran both ways. **Why this is worth knowing when you are learning.** It explains what to take from where. If you want to render form, study the people who spent centuries solving it. If you want colour used optically, look at the Impressionists. If you want composition, Japanese prints will teach you more in an afternoon than most textbooks. And it removes the beginner's anxiety about which style is correct: they are tools for different jobs, and the question is what you are trying to do.
